rationale: A wins because it makes the strongest story the evidence gap, not Khan's flattering metric: "Khan Academy's AI tutor reaches 1 million more students before the research is in" is the frame a real education reporter can defend. B is competent, but "An AI tutor's own pilot data: regular users gained the equivalent of extra weeks of learning" still lets a self-measured, non-peer-reviewed result sit too cleanly in the headline. Both found the same four lanes; A is sharper about what can backfire.
gaps_in_A: "The prevailing belief is that a nonprofit's free tool sidesteps the scrutiny applied to commercial edtech" is plausible, but not supplied. Make it a question, not a fact.
"A donor-funded nonprofit is giving away AI tutoring that competitors sell" leans on competitor context the update did not provide.
"the pilot districts have a full stretch of classroom use behind them" overstates the timeline; the update only says there were pilot districts with classroom results.
gaps_in_B: "one of the largest AI-tutoring deployments" is invented. The update gives 1 million additional students, not market rank.
"while the rest of ed-tech charges per seat" overclaims. The facts do not establish how the rest of the market prices AI tutoring.
"a real, named counter-belief here" is sloppy because the update only says "some educators question" the effect on independent thinking. No named critic was supplied.
The lead data headline foregrounds "regular users gained the equivalent of extra weeks of learning" before the caveats. That is how a company-produced number gets laundered into a cleaner finding.
